About this routine

This routine was made because I saw that all of the free beginner bodyweight routines out there were lacking. Of course, they work, in fact almost anything you do will work as a beginner. But I thought I could do better. Here's how this routine is different.

  1. Simple and smooth progressions allow you to easily keep to a rep range and keep volume consistent.
  2. A-B-A B-A-B scheduling allows you to keep workouts short while still getting enough volume, frequency and variety to make solid gains.
  3. 5x5 rep scheme has been widely considered the best for beginner programs for the last century or so. Optimum gains in both strength and hypertrophy will occur.
  4. Modulation allows you to adapt the routine to your wants and needs, without the risk of you screwing anything up.
  5. Sufficient leg training [lacking in basically every routine out there] keeps you from turning into a "captain upper body". And it's all done with bodyweight so you won't turn into a "centaur" either.

That's enough of that. Let's get to the routine.

The Routine

All you really need to do this routine is a pullup bar, but a pair of rings or workout straps are highly recommended. If you can't get those you can just use a rope to do your rows [and face pulls if you want them], but again, they're highly recommended. Look up how to make some yourself, it's pretty easy and beats the hell out of just a rope. Also, if you want to do the chest flies, you'll need either a pair of furniture sliders and a carpeted floor, or a pair of soft rags and a hard wood/tile floor. Either works just fine.

The routine is divided into two workouts, workout A and workout B. You'll work out three non-consecutive days of the week, with the days inbetween off and two consecutive days at the end off too. For most people this will mean working out Monday, Wednesday, and Friday with Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday off. But if you have a weird schedule and you want to work out Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday with Wednesday, Friday, Sunday and Monday off, that's fine too. You will do each workout every other time you workout. So one week you will do workouts A-B-A, and the next you will do B-A-B, then A-B-A again, then B-A-B again, and so on.

Workout A

  • Warmup
  • [Optional] Skill Work- see below
  • [Optional] Explosive/Power work- High Jumps and Kipping Pullups, 5x2 each
  • Main Exercise 1- Pushup progression, 5x5
  • Main Exercise 2- Row progression, 5x5
  • [Optional] Arm Isolation/Hypertrophy work- bicep curls and tricep extensions, 2 sets of 10-20 each
  • Main Exercise 3- Shrimp Squat Progression, 5x5
  • [Optional] Direct Ab Work, see below
  • [Optional] Burnout- Sprints

Workout B

  • Warmup
  • [Optional] Skill Work- see below
  • [Optional] Explosive/Power work- Long Jumps and Explosive Pushups, 5x2 each
  • Main Exercise 1- Handstand pushup progression, 5x5
  • Main Exercise 2- Pullup Progression, 5x5
  • [Optional] Chest and Back Isolation/Hypertrophy Work- Bodyweight chest flies and face pulls, 2 sets of 10-20 each
  • Main Exercise 3- Glute-ham raise progression, 5x5
  • [Optional] Direct calf work, leaning calf raises, 100 reps ALRAP
  • [Optional] Burnout- Burpees- descending sets

The Exercises

This section will be dedicated to teaching you how to progress all of the exercises as smoothly as possible for optimum gains, and how to do all the modules, like the warmup and the burnouts.

The Warmup

The warmup is fairly simple. Just lightly jog or skip rope for a few minutes to get your blood flowing to your extremities, and then do a couple of easy sets of an easy progression of the three main exercises you are doing for that day. Try to pick variations you could do for 20 reps, and then do them for 7-10. Do one set of one warmup exercise at a time, and then move on to the next one, and then the final one, and then repeat. Doing this makes it quicker. Don't wear yourself out, this isn't supposed to be challenging.

Skill Work

Unlike some other beginner routines, this one won't tell you what to do for your skill work. The simple reason for this is that I don't know you, or what sports/activites you may or may not do, or what you're interested in. If you do parkour, maybe you want to practice your wall climbs or your landing rolls. That's cool. If you're a martial artist maybe you want to practice your jab, or your flying spinning back kick. That's cool too. Keep in mind that all of these things are just as much bodyweight fitness as the gymnastics stuff some people tell you to practice are. If you can't think of anything neat that you want to practice, and you just want to look better, then don't do any skill work at all, simple as that.

Explosive power work

I picked four exercises for this, two with a focus on the upper body and two with a focus on the lower body, to give you complete explosive strength overall. This modulation is not recommended unless you are already fairly fit and can do regular pullups and pushups already, and you can jump more than a foot in the air and not have your knees hurt afterwards. If you're not there yet, leave this out for now.

Long jump- Stand and jump as far as you can. Progress by jumping further. If you want to measure this, you can use sticks in the dirt, or chalk on concrete. The Grand Canyon's the limit.

High jump- Stand and jump as high as you can. Progress by jumping higher. If you want to measure this you can do so by marking a wall from the highest point of your jump with a sharpie or some chalk. The sky's the limit.

Explosive pushup- get in a pushup position, dip down slightly [NOT all the way], and push up explosively. You can measure your progression by clapping, first in front of you, then behind your back, then maybe overhead, then maybe a triple clap. This is really just to show off or keep yourself entertained, the real gains come just from pushing harder. You could do jazz hands in the air and it would make no difference in the end.

Kipping pullup- a combination of a kip and a pull, this exercise will eventually lead to a muscle up. Progress by kipping harder and pulling higher until eventually you're over the bar. If you get a muscle up and want to progress past that, you can do a strict explosive pullup/muscleup, which eliminates the kip, or a straight-armed kip/muscle up, which eliminates the pull. Ideally you'd alternate between the two. Alternately you could work on a one arm kipping pullup with the goal of a one arm muscle up. I've only seen one guy do this on youtube but it was 90% kip, and he used a thin, bendy bar which I can imagine would help out a lot.

Pushup progression

To progress to pushups, start on a large incline and lower yourself bit by bit, workout after workout, until you can do them on the ground. Keep your hands shoulder width throughout all this.Once you can do 5x5 perfect reps, go back to the incline, but do one arm pushups. Then lower yourself again. Once you can do 5x5 perfect one arm pushups from the ground, you're not a beginner anymore. Realistically this would take years since perfect one arm pushups are very rare. For the incline, rings or straps are very useful because they let you lower yourself as incrementally as you could possibly hope for. If you don't have those you'll have to improvise, and adjust your form to help you get 5x5 with the bumpier progression [widening your legs makes it easier, closing them makes it harder].

Handstand pushups progression

To get to handstand pushups. you'll start with pike pushups, which is like a pushup with your butt up in the air and your head pointing down towards the ground. Keeping your hands shoulder width apart, you lower yourself until your noggin touches the floor, and then push back up. Done with your hands three feet in front of your toes, they are easier than regular pushups. Get your hands closer to your toes and they get much harder. When your hands get so close to your toes that your balance starts to suffer, begin elevating your feet. Once your feet are waist height and your body's at a perfect 90 degree angle with your torso facing down, and you get a perfect 5x5 like this, you are ready for handstand pushups. Kick up against a wall and do them, keeping your hands wider than shoulder width. To progress from here, work on moving your hands closer and closer together, workout by workout. When you get to the end of this progression and can do diamond handstand pushups, you're definitely not a beginner anymore.

Row progression

Exactly like the pushup progression, just inverted. Start at an incline row and lower yourself over time, eventually doing rows with no incline, then move onto incline one arm rows, and lower yourself again. When you get a perfect 5x5 of one arm rows [this means controlled, full ROM and perfect form, feet together], you're no longer a beginner.

Thank you, yes it took me several hours and I'm quite proud of it. I don't think there's anything else out there quite like it.

Ah yes, form, you've touched on a sensitive topic here. To me, form is essential in demonstrating mastery of an exercise [for example, no one will say you've mastered one arm pushups if your legs are double shoulder width apart and your torso is bent way the hell over and you only dip halfway down] but similarly, bad form is also essential, in the beginning of doing those same exercises. Because when you start off doing those same one arm pushups, while your form shouldn't be as bad as I previously described, there's simply no way it will be perfect either. In this way, bad form is not only necessary, it's completely unavoidable to the advancing bodyweight athlete.

Let me qualify all of this by saying that weightlifting is completely different from bodyweight, and that in weightlifting, form is far more important, as it prevents possible injury in things like the squat and the deadlift, where the body is under extreme loads and a small break in form can cause catastrophic injury. You simply don't have this in bodyweight as the body is never really under any greater load than it's own weight; one of the main advantages of bodyweight is how much safer it is. People who do bodyweight and are anal about form are usually ex-weightlifters, and this once-essential but no longer necessary ideology simply carries over.

One more thing. In weightlifting there is simply no need to cheat on form, as the exercise never changes, there is no progression, it is always the same exercise, just with more weight. Likewise, in the early progressions of this bodyweight program there is no need to cheat on form either, as the progression is, for the most part, completely smooth. Like in pushups, just subtract a little more incline at a time and keep your form good throughout. It is only when making "jumps" in progression that bad form is needed, like in the final jump to the floor in one-arm pushups, or in the jump from hands together pullups to archer pullups [no WAY those are going to be perfect when you start out]. And that bad form should always be a temporary thing that you are constantly working to straighten out in order to truly master the exercise.

Finally, while the potential for injury in bodyweight exercise is minimal, especially compared to weightlifting, it's always there and you should always take care of yourself. While bad form isn't going to hurt you 99% of the time, if you do find yourself doing something that is causing you pain you should stop, step back, and reexamine what you are doing, and find another way to go about it that doesn't hurt you.

Pullup progression

If you can't do a pullup yet, do them with your feet on a box underneath you, and use your legs to assist you. Make sure to use a full range of motion. Over time, move the box further out in front of you, until only your toes are on it, just barely assisting you. Once you get a solid 5x5 like this, remove the box completely and use a kip to help you out. If you start out with kipping pullups and can only get 1-4 per set, do the remainder as negatives, jumping to get your chin over the bar. Eventually you'll get a perfect 5x5 of kipping pullups. From here, simply work on reducing the kip, until it becomes just a shift in the legs, then goes away completely. Okay, now you're at 5x5 of perfect, strict pullups with your chin over the bar, yes? Now begin moving your hands closer together. This works mostly by increasing the range of motion, so don't worry about it affecting your muscle growth. Once you get 5x5 of perfect, hands together pullups, start on archer pullups. At first this will mean pulling only slightly towards one hand, but over time you can straighten the off-hand out until you are doing perfect archer pullups with the off-arm straight at the top. Note that 5x5 for this, and other unilaterals, means 5x5 PER SIDE. Once you get 5x5 perfect archer pullups, you're not a beginner anymore, so I won't cover past that here.

Isolation exercises

Like the explosive exercises, this modulation is not recommended if you are highly out of shape. Focus on losing weight first, since the muscles these help grow won't even matter if you're too fat to tell.

Bicep curls- the way I recommend doing these is to find something sturdy to hook your hands under and do ledge curls, using your biceps to pull your upper body down to the ledge, and resisting with your back. If you can find a place to do these you'll never run out of strength progression with this one movement, since your biceps will never become stronger than your lower back. If you can't find a place to do these, you can do row curls instead. That's essentially an underhand row in which you do not allow your elbow to move from a fixed position, usually by your side. They can be progressed exactly like normal rows, only easier progressions will be much harder since the strong back muscles are taken out of the equation.

Triceps extensions- these are done quite easily with your hands on either your rings/straps or an object a bit out in front of you. They are done like a pushup where your elbow is not allowed to move, taking the chest out of the equation. They are progressed by taking weight of your feet and putting onto your triceps, by leaning forwards, essentially. Doing them out in front of you helps to make the movement feel more natural.

Flies- done with cloth on a hard floor or furniture sliders on carpet, these are done from a pushup position. Move your hands out to the side until your chest touches the ground, then squeeeeze your pectoral muscles and pull your hands back inwards until you are in a pushup position again. Progression is as simple as bending our elbows less. Slowing down the eccentric portion of the movement helps too. Once you can do these with perfectly straight arms and a ten second eccentric.... well, I've been doing them or years and I haven't gotten there yet.

Face pulls- exactly like rows, only you pull to your face instead of your sides. These work the rear delts, which help improve your posture, and help counterbalance all the chest and tricep work, which, if done on it's own, tends to make you slouch forward in posture. Not good. One thing though, once you get these perfect at 2 sets of 20 with no incline, I recommend elevating your feet and slowing down the eccentric to progress, instead of doing one arms. These just don't work so well one-armed, in my experience.

Shrimp squat progression

A shrimp squat is a single-legged squat where you are holding the non-working leg behind you, and you touch your non-working knee to the ground at the bottom of the exercise. To progress to these, start with a "skater squat", which is like a shrimp squat where your arms are in front of you the whole time. If you can't do these yet, allow your off foot to kick the ground at the bottom of the exercise to help push you off. Depending on how much you let it help, this can make these as easy as a lunge. Let it help less over time, until you can do 5x5 good skater squats. At this point, progressing is as simple as moving your hand on the side of the non-working leg back towards it, until eventually you're grabbing it and doing a shrimp squat. The beautiful simplicity of progression is why I love these things, compared to pistols, which are much more complicated to progress. Once you get 5x5 good shrimp squats, you can begin moving the other hand back, until you are grabbing the off foot with both hands and doing what is known as a "jumbo shrimp squat". These are insanely difficult and if you get them you're not a beginner anymore.

Glute-ham raise progression

This wonderfully simple exercise is done by sticking your feet under something solid in a kneeling position, and lowering your body to the ground, then pushing back up. With time you can push less and less until you are doing these unassisted, with your hands across your chest. Doing this is fairly advanced on it's own, but to progress even further, you can work on getting your hands above your head, bending less at the waist, and slowing the eccentric. Legends abound on the internet of people being able to do these with one leg, but I haven't seen it and I don't believe it. One more thing, these can be hard on the knees, unless you stick something soft under them. I recommend a folded up towel.

Direct ab work

There are dozens of great ab exercises out there, and I'm sure everyone wants to master a different one. They all work, but here are two good ones.

Dragon flags- my personal favorite, and that of Bruce Lee, is an exercise where you lie down, lock your hands under something solid above your head, pull your legs up to face the ceiling, and then lower back down, slowly, keeping your body as straight as possible throughout. There are a lot of bad examples out there, but truely good dragon flags are a sight to behold. Progression is as simple as straightening yourself out further and slowing the eccentric.

Hanging leg raises- to do these, you start off doing hanging knee raises, and straighten your legs over time, until you can do them to 90 degrees with perfectly straight legs. But there's no need to stop there. You can work to raising your legs all the way to the bar you are hanging from, and moving them side to side, ala "windshield wipers". Some can even do these hanging from only one arm, an absolute oblique killer.

Direct calf work

Okay, first, a couple things about the calves. First, the calves are typically used in nature in a forward leaning position [watch someone sprint], which is why I recommend the exercise that I do. It's a matter of being functional, of not going against nature. Secondly, the calves love volume, which is why fat people get big calves just from walking around, and why I recommend doing 100 reps in one giant pause-set with as little rest as possible.

To do leaning calf raises, just lean into a doorway and push up against it, and do calf raises. It's the best way I've found thus far to do calf raises with just your bodyweight. You can alter the resistance by pushing harder or less hard. Just try your best to keep it consistent within each session. Don't go easy on yourself at rep 80 because your calves are begging for mercy. Your growth will thank you.

Burnout

This modulation is mainly for those who want to improve their conditioning, and get some high intensity cardio in for heart health. It may also help burn fat slightly more than the workout would otherwise, but of course it's no replacement for a proper diet, which is 95% of losing weight. Also, it's pretty intense, so the highly out of shape may want to lean out some first, or at least go eay on themselves. Okay, here are the two exercises I've deemed best for this.

Sprinting- Sprinting is incredible high intensity cardio, and it even helps build mass in the legs. Sprinting is a bit more complicated than any of the other exercises in this program, so check out my write-up I already did on it here. If you find you really like sprinting and want to do better at it, cut the ab work if you were doing it, and do two less sets of the shrimp squats, so 3x5.

Burpees- burpees are the only form of cardio I can think of that rival sprinting in sheer make-you-think-you're-going-to-pass-out intensity. They're done, as I'm sure you remember from gym class, by squatting down, putting your hands out in front of you, kicking your legs back, doing a pushup, kicking your legs back in, and jumping. Then repeating for reps. The way to do these for burnout cardio is in descending sets, which means doing a number, then resting for the amount of time that set took you, and then doing the next set with one less rep, working your way down to a set of one rep. At first, descending sets of seven or eight may be enough to challenge you. To up the intensity, try working up to descending sets of 20 or even 30.

One More Thing [this wouldn't fit on the end, voat has a 10,000 character limit for posts]

Since I'm sure people are going to ask, "how can I do this routine more quickly?", here are some options to fit it in specified periods of time.

One hour- Do the warmup, the three main exercises for the day, and maybe one or two optionals if you can. Move briskly through the workout.

45 minutes- Do just the warmup and the three main exercises. Try to stick to 5x5, but switch to 3x8 if needed. Move quickly through the workout.

Half and hour- Only do one warmup set instead of two for each exercise. Do 3x8 instead of 5x5 for each of the three main exercises. Move hurriedly through the workout.

Fifteen minutes- do only some bodyweight squats as a warmup, do one set to failure of 12-18 of each of the three movements. Really not recommended, but better than nothing.
